title: Tree trunk diameter must grow as the 3/2 power of height

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Tree trunk diameter must grow as the 3/2 power of height

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: For a tree to stand without buckling under its own weight, its diameter must increase as the 3/2 power of its height, which explains why young trees are slender and old large ones stunted, and sets a theoretical maximum tree height (about 300 ft for a Kew-flagstaff pine).

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: d \propto h^{3/2} (no buckling under own weight); h_{max} \approx 300\,\text{ft} for the Kew-flagstaff pine

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: In general, as Greenhill shews, the diameter of a homogeneous body must increase as the power 3/2 of the height, which accounts for the slender proportions of young trees, compared with the stunted appearance of old and large ones.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter II, “On Magnitude”; topic “Height limits of trees”. Scope: trees and other tall self-supporting plant stems

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: d \propto h^{3/2} (no buckling under own weight); h_{max} \approx 300\,\text{ft} for the Kew-flagstaff pine

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch02-02: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.70

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The exponent is directly testable, and substantial tree trait and census data exist. Testing the exact buckling explanation and maximum height requires harmonizing mechanical traits and architecture, while the law's homogeneous-body assumptions restrict applicability.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Fit log trunk diameter against log height within and across tree species and test whether the slope is 1.5, then evaluate buckling safety factors using wood density and elastic modulus. Strongly different slopes or trees stable beyond the predicted buckling boundary would refute the stated law.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Taper, branching, wind loading and species-specific wood properties violate homogeneity.

Diameter and height are not always measured together openly.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Diameter and height for hundreds of thousands of trees are already in open allometric tables, and a log-log comparison with the rival exponents 1 and 2 is a standard regression. That decides the scaling law that is the core of the claim, including the relative slenderness of smaller stems. The single-pine height of about 300 ft needs a modulus the density database does not supply, and several mechanical models can share an exponent, but neither gap blocks a clear test of the stated 3/2 relation.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Regress log stem diameter on log height. An exponent near 3/2 would support elastic similarity; exponents near 1 or 2 would favor geometric similarity or constant-stress scaling instead. The separate numerical cap of about 300 ft is checked by inserting the measured taper, density, and modulus of a pine of the Kew-flagstaff form into Greenhill's buckling formula.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Wind and hydraulics predict exponents similar to elastic buckling, and elastic modulus is not in the density table.

Inventories are cross-sectional, so young-versus-old slenderness is inferred from size rather than from followed stems.
